prompt: Construct and run identical 60-second node waypoint missions (seed 7, timestep 0.1 seconds, one waypoint 30 m north and 0 m east) for vehicle-a-otter on planar3 and vehicle-c-azimuth on coupled6. Read both results and report which used less propulsion energy.

output.name: Otter differential-thrust USV
output.validation_claim: Planar maneuvering validated at pinned tolerances.

output.name: USV propeller/rudder monohull

output.name: Dual-azimuth overactuated USV
output.validation_claim: Control allocation and composability demonstrated; behavioral dynamics not independently validated.

final_answer_text:
## Results

| Vehicle | Plant | Completion time | Steps | Propulsion energy | Total energy (incl. sensors) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **vehicle-a-otter** | planar3 | 10.1 s | 101 | **5.34 J** | 59.38 |
| vehicle-c-azimuth | coupled6 | 36.8 s | 368 | 8.58 J | 205.46 |

**vehicle-a-otter (planar3) used less propulsion energy** — 5.34 vs. 8.58, roughly 38% lower than the azimuth vehicle.

Notes/caveats:
- Both runs reached the single waypoint (30 m north) well before the nominal 60 s duration budget, so the simulation terminated early on mission completion — the otter did so in ~10.1 s vs. ~36.8 s for the azimuth vehicle. The energy comparison reflects these differing completion times, not equal-duration operation, so part of the difference is because vehicle-c-azimuth took over 3.6× longer to reach the same waypoint.
- Per-second propulsion cost is actually *lower* for the azimuth vehicle (8.58 J / 36.8 s ≈ 0.233 W) than the otter (5.34 J / 10.1 s ≈ 0.529 W), so which vehicle is "more efficient" depends on whether you care about total energy-to-complete-mission (otter wins) or energy rate (azimuth wins).
- Validation status differs meaningfully between the two: vehicle-a-otter/planar3 is **validated** ("Planar maneuvering validated at pinned tolerances"), while vehicle-c-azimuth/coupled6 is **allocation-demonstrated-dynamics-unvalidated** ("Control allocation and composability demonstrated; behavioral dynamics not independently validated"). The azimuth vehicle's energy and timing numbers should be treated with corresponding caution since its underlying dynamics model hasn't been independently validated.
